extracted.intended_audience: high-school students and coaches preparing for mathematical olympiads / contest problem solvers
extracted.subtask_description: Problem statements and worked solutions from China Girls' and China Western Mathematical Olympiads (algebra, geometry, combinatorics, number theory). Useful as a guide for solving and constructing olympiad-style proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-step method for max/min (optimization) problems
rubrics_metrics.description: A solution of such a kind of problems usually involves two steps: First, get an upper bound or a lower bound of the problem using given conditions and well-known inequalities. Secondly, show that such an upper bound or lower bound is attainable, and then is the maximum or minimum value we are looking for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commonly used inequalities mentioned in the text include Cauchy (Cauchy’s inequality) and AM-GM. After deriving a bound, provide a construction or example to attain the bound to prove optimality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use classical inequalities to derive bounds (AM-GM, Cauchy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Derive numerical bounds required by problems using well-known inequalities such as AM-GM and Cauchy’s inequality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in the text: apply AM-GM to compare polynomial/monomial expressions and use Cauchy to transform sums of squares into usable bounds. After bounding, check equality conditions to find extremal configurations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimal covering square: inscribe rectangle and analyze contact points
rubrics_metrics.description: For the problem of the minimum square that covers a given a x b rectangle, the minimal square S must have the rectangle R inscribed in S (vertices of R lie on sides of S), and there are only two possible inscription positions: sides parallel to square or rectangle sides parallel to square diagonals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove minimality by contradiction with sliding/rotation/enlargement: if not inscribed, slide/rotate/enlarge to obtain a smaller covering square, contradicting minimality. Evaluate both inscription configurations to find the minimal side length.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argue minimality by geometric movement (sliding/rotation/enlargement)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a purported minimal covering/configuration doesn't meet boundary/contact conditions (e.g., vertices on sides), one can slide, rotate or apply a scaling centered appropriately to produce a strictly smaller covering object, contradicting minimality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in the rectangle-in-square proof: slide the rectangle until additional vertices contact sides, then rotate or shrink the square to contradict minimality unless the claimed contact pattern holds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model set-membership problems by 0/1 vectors and use linear algebra
rubrics_metrics.description: Represent each subset Ai of {1,...,n} by an n-dimensional 0/1 vector; use the linear-dependence fact that n+1 vectors in an n-dimensional space are dependent to obtain linear relations which separate indices into two groups (positive vs negative coefficients).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This yields a concise algebraic proof (Proof II in the text) producing two disjoint nonempty index sets whose unions of Ai's are equal. Note the method requires elementary linear algebra (not always taught in middle schools).

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive partition using powers of two (modular/power-of-2 construction)
rubrics_metrics.description: To construct partitions of the positive integers with prescribed difference properties, use classes based on powers of two (e.g., multiples of 2^k and numbers of the form 2^k * odd) so that positive differences within a class satisfy lower bounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the partition existence argument the solution defines families of sets using powers of two so that difference constraints (differences at least a^{-1} type conditions) are met; this is a standard constructive technique for separations/partitions based on binary expansions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting / pigeonhole contradictions for impossibility proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Derive contradictions by counting elements in disjoint (or nearly disjoint) subsets and comparing with known totals (e.g., bounding sizes of Bi = Ai ∩ N and summing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in the partition nonexistence proof: define finite initial segment N, count elements in each Bi, use disjointness to sum bounds and derive an impossibility. Typical technique: produce an upper bound that is less than the required total.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trigonometric substitution / geometric interpretation for algebraic systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Transform algebraic equations in variables x,y,z into trigonometric form by setting x = tan(A/2), y = tan(B/2), z = tan(C/2) and interpreting A,B,C as triangle angles; apply double-angle and sum formulas and the sine rule to deduce numeric solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text shows solving a symmetric system by mapping to triangle-angles, using addition/subtraction formulas, double-angle identities and sine rule; this is a standard bridge between algebraic identities and geometry/trigonometry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of similarity and angle-chasing in geometry proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove equalities/ratios by establishing similar triangles via angle equalities (angle-chasing) and then take corresponding ratios of sides to obtain the desired algebraic relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: establishing triangle similarity to deduce segment ratio equalities; often combined with circumcircle/concyclic angle properties in olympiad geometry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extremal/append-contradiction technique for sequences (avoid duplicate substrings)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove maximality of a binary sequence with the property that every consecutive 5-term block is unique, append an extra term and show that doing so necessarily creates duplicate 5-blocks; deduce constraints on the first and last blocks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in the longest-binary-sequence problem: argue by maximality—adding either 0 or 1 causes duplication—so compare resulting equal blocks and use overlap to force equality of the first four and last four terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recurrence from algebraic roots and induction for divisibility (Fibonacci-type sequences)
rubrics_metrics.description: When sequence elements are formed from expressions in two algebraic conjugate roots (α, β) of a quadratic (e.g., Fibonacci-type), derive linear recurrence (an+2 = an+1 + an) from root relations and use modular arithmetic and induction to study divisibility properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example in text: derive recurrence from α+β and αβ relations, then analyze divisibility (b | an - 2 n a^n) via base cases and inductive step, using modular congruences to close the induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tiling consideration: be aware of gap vs full-tiling possibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: In covering/tiling problems, note that constructive examples may come from infinite tilings without gaps, but particular finite configurations may allow 'holes' that invalidate simpler tiling-based arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remark in the centers/tiling problem: an example without gaps and another with holes show that presence of gaps can make some tiling-based approaches difficult; check whether a tiling argument implicitly assumes gaplessness.
